1:
What the people complained of is never said, and the sources fill the silence differently. Gill records the usual guess that it was the journey, then objects that eight miles could hardly tire them when they were marching toward Canaan, and passes on Jarchi's reading that the word means seeking an occasion, as men looking for a pretext to separate from the Lord. Henry supposes the complainers did not agree among themselves, some fretting that they had left Sinai where they had rested and others that they had not left sooner, some at the weather and some at the roads, and concludes that a discontented spirit will always find something to quarrel with. Clarke reports Jerome's conjecture of the length of the way and Wesley the three days through a howling wilderness with the dread of many more, while Keil and Delitzsch decline to name a cause at all and read it as general dissatisfaction uttered so loudly that it reached the ears of God.

Calvin makes the difficulty a matter of grammar, since the participle is ambiguous and translators have twisted it accordingly. He lists the renderings offered, complaining or murmuring, being sick, which he thinks savours of affectation, dealing treacherously, and seeking occasion, which he rejects as far fetched. His own choice is fainting, that they failed as men broken down with weariness, and that no other crime is charged than the supineness which turns its back on God and repudiates the promised inheritance. He does not deny they broke into open reproaches as well, since Moses says the thing displeased the ears of God and not his eyes, and Ellicott presses the same phrase, preferring that the people were as those who complained, which was evil in the ears of the Lord.

On the fire itself the sources divide over its nature. Henry takes it for such flashes from the cloud as had consumed Nadab and Abihu, and finds a justice in it, that the fire of their wrath against God burned in their minds before the fire of his wrath fastened on their bodies. Clarke offers three possibilities, a supernatural fire, commissioned lightning, or one of the hot suffocating winds of that country, and Ellicott mentions the simoom by name, while Keil and Delitzsch will only say that it was sent by God without proceeding directly from him as at the death of Aaron's sons. Its extent is disputed too, Clarke arguing that it must have reached every murmurer wherever he stood, whereas Calvin conjectures that God kindled it at an extremity to awaken terror and leave room for pardon, and Wesley and Henry both read the sparing of the camp's centre as mercy meant to warn rather than destroy.

Calvin draws the sharpest lesson from what followed, that the people cried to Moses and not to God because a guilty conscience had shut the door against their own prayers. Being without repentance or faith they dreaded to look on God, which he calls the reward of a bad conscience, to seek rest in our disquiet while still flying from the only one who can allay it. Henry reaches the same point by another road, that those who slight God's friends in prosperity are glad to claim them in distress, and adds that the swiftness of the answer shows God takes no delight in punishing. Ellicott and Calvin agree the fire was not so much quenched as made to sink down, and Wesley closes on the name, noting that the same camp would earn a second one before the chapter ended, both of them monuments of the people's sin and of God's just judgment.
4:
Clarke and Ellicott both start from the word for the mixed multitude, a term for people gathered or collected, which Ellicott thinks often means the children of Hebrew women by Egyptian fathers. Gill notes the Targum calls them proselytes, and Clarke less kindly a mongrel people with little knowledge of God. Keil and Delitzsch put the first impulse there too, and hear in the phrase that they wept again a backward reference to the complaint in the wilderness of Sin, where no weeping is actually recorded. Henry supplies the sharpest image, that these hangers-on were the leaven that leavened the lump, and warns that a few discontented people can do great mischief in the best society. Calvin draws the double lesson, that the wicked are to be avoided since vice spreads by contagion, and that instigation by others excuses nobody, since Israel's own lust carried them away.

Henry has no patience with what they remembered, since men who had sighed under their burdens now talked as though they had lived like princes, recalling the cucumbers but never the brick-kilns. Gill supports the picture from Herodotus and Diodorus, that the Nile teemed with fish, while insisting Israel had paid dearly for that food in hard service. Clarke defends the taste of the complainers, granting a European may smile at such delicacies but holding that there the onions and garlic differ as much from ours as a bad turnip from a good apple. Ellicott adds that Egyptian watermelons moderate the heat of the climate and the onions are reckoned the sweetest in the world.

Whether they ate it freely divides the sources. Wesley takes it for nothing or very little, suspecting the price was low because the Egyptians would not touch fish or the leeks and onions they worshipped. Ellicott restricts the word to the fish and glosses it as gratuitously rather than abundantly, while Calvin cites Raphelius on the Egyptian custom of paying labourers in onions and garlic. He also refuses to hear the list as one of luxuries, judging that lowly people were praising their accustomed fare, since rustics value their cheese and cabbage as highly as the rich value sumptuous cooking.

Against this the sources set the manna, which Henry describes as bread from heaven that cost neither money nor care, fell while they slept, and left them seemingly exempt from the curse of eating bread in the sweat of the face. They had once admired it and now despised it, which is his standing complaint against a peevish mind, that it finds fault with what has no fault except being too good for it. Gill, Wesley and Calvin agree the comparison to coriander seed is one of shape and not colour, since coriander is dark and the manna white, and Wesley and Calvin take the bdellium for a pearl where Clarke declines to guess. Ellicott alone presses the point into a figure, that the craving of Israel for the more stimulating food of Egypt answers to man's natural repugnance to the spiritual food of the gospel.

Calvin raises the question the passage forces, whether it can be sinful to long for flesh, since on that principle every appetite is condemned. His answer names three faults and not the desire itself, that they wanted flesh against God's will, that they lusted a lust and threw off restraint, and that they were ungrateful for angels' food. Henry reaches the same distinction otherwise, that flesh is lawful food and yet what is lawful becomes evil when God has not allotted it, and that we should indulge no desire we cannot in faith turn into prayer. He adds that the question who will give us flesh assumed God could not, which is letting our desires outrun our faith, while Wesley notes their cattle were reserved for breeding and too few to feed them a month.
10:
Gill measures the weeping by the fact that it was loud enough for Moses to hear across the whole camp, family by family at every tent door. Calvin calls the display almost prodigious, asking what these men would have done in a real famine gnawing bitter roots, and takes it for a lesson that indulged appetite makes people wretched in the midst of prosperity. He adds that grief of this kind is largely self-inflicted, since an evil that endurance would lighten is made heavier by preposterous imagining. Ellicott prefers to render the next clause as it was evil in the eyes of Moses, noting that the verb is the same one used of the Lord in the previous line, and that Moses felt unequal to the weight of his responsibility.

Whether Moses was right to speak so is the question the sources really argue. Henry allows the provocation was very great and still holds that Moses spoke otherwise than became him, undervaluing the honour God had put on him, magnifying his own performance, and speaking distrustfully of grace which could have carried him through a far heavier work. Calvin agrees the zeal itself was holy but the excess an error, since a man who had experienced God's aid whenever he groaned under his burden had no room left for complaint. Keil and Delitzsch draw the finest distinction, that this is the discontent of despair rather than the murmuring of unbelief, because it is addressed to God and asks him for help, where unbelief complains of his ways without praying to him at all.

On the question whether he had conceived the people, Ellicott notes that the pronoun is emphatic in both clauses, and Wesley puts the sense bluntly, that they were not his children and he was not bound to provide for their necessity and their desire. Gill concedes the literal point and denies the inference, since every governor is in a civil sense the father of his country and owes it a father's care, and he passes on Ainsworth's observation that no one is regenerated by the law of Moses at all. Calvin is harsher, calling the question inconsiderate, as though a divine calling laid a man under no obligation and there were no ties but those of nature. Gill and Ellicott both wince at the next words, Gill because they seem to countenance the lusting as though the people's demand were reasonable, and Ellicott because Moses, who certainly knew the murmuring was sinful, nevertheless writes as if their request were not.

The claim to be alone is qualified by three of the sources, Gill pointing to the Lord's own presence in every hard case, Ellicott and Wesley to the able men chosen on Jethro's advice, who settled small matters but were no use in a crisis like this. Ellicott adds a textual note of some weight, that my wretchedness is one of the eighteen places where the scribes are said to have altered the text, putting my for Thy. Keil and Delitzsch read the request for death as an unbroken process of killing and take the misfortune to be the calamity Moses expected eventually to succumb to, while Wesley traces the dread to the fear that Israel's extirpation would make both Moses and God look like impostors. Calvin calls this the grossest fault in the whole complaint, the longing of despair to be removed from the world so that death may end our troubles, and asks what may happen to us when impatience could carry away God's most chosen servant.
16:
Gill and Keil and Delitzsch both notice that God answers without upbraiding a servant whose words bordered on despair, and Keil and Delitzsch hold the complaint had good ground, since the office really was too heavy for one man and the discontent was zeal for it rather than weariness of it. Henry reads the relief the same way, that Moses is not discarded but given assistants, God's goodness taking occasion from man's badness to appear the more illustrious. Moses himself names the seventy, he notes, the people being too heady to be trusted with an election, and is to choose men who are elders indeed and not in name only. Both Henry and Clarke connect the number with the later Sanhedrin, though Clarke resists the rabbinic claim that it began here, a council of seventy having existed a year earlier.

The phrase about taking of the spirit that was on Moses draws one answer by three routes. Clarke reports that Origen and Theodoret likened Moses to a lamp at which seventy others were lit without loss of brightness, and Ellicott cites Rashi on the lighting of the sanctuary lamps from the golden candlestick. Wesley insists the spirit came to them immediately from God and not through Moses, so nothing was taken from him, and explains the gift as prophecy, which made them fit to govern. Clarke alone will not leave it there, asking whether Moses did lose some measure of what he had, and warning that gifts undervalued may be taken away and given to those who use them better.

Ellicott finds the command to sanctify themselves striking, since the request granted was a sinful one answered in judgment more than mercy, as the psalm says of leanness sent into the soul. Calvin takes the word as irony outright, chastisement of brutal gluttony rather than a call to purity, and rejects the blunter paraphrase that makes it mean only whet your teeth and make ready your bellies. Wesley reads it more hopefully as a call to repentance, that they might obtain some mitigation, or their souls be saved while their bodies perished by the flesh they craved. Henry treats the promised month as a threat, and draws from it the vanity of sensual delights, which cloy without satisfying, so that God justly makes loathsome what men inordinately desire.

Wesley states the principle as a rule, that God destroys them by granting their desires and turns their blessings into curses, and presses the aggravation of sinning before a judge resident among them. Calvin builds his argument on that clause, that having despised a God in the midst of them they cannot plead inadvertency, since men who knew by experience where their food came from were despising a beneficence in plain view. His conclusion is that the more immediately God shows his grace, the less excusable we are in disparaging it. Ellicott adds that the quails of the previous year had covered the camp a single day, and Gill notes the Jewish inference that Israel stayed a full month at that camp.

Moses answers with arithmetic, and the sources agree it was a failure of faith. Henry likens it to the disciples asking whence a man could satisfy so many, and observes that Moses reckoned on beasts or fish as the bulkiest creatures, little thinking small birds would serve. Calvin allows the motive was pious, a fear that God's name would be derided, but names two faults, that he did not simply trust and that he measured an inestimable power by his own senses. Ellicott notes that no article marks the flocks as Israel's own and calls the question a natural hyperbole, while Wesley asks why this distrust went unpunished and answers that it was a first offence spoken in private, where the later one was public.
24:
Calvin measures the rebuke's success by the obedience, since doubt had stopped Moses mid-course and his promptitude now shows the distrust overcome. Henry says the same of his temper, that a man disturbed by the tumult was composed again by communion with God, and set the elders before the Lord so the people might witness their call. Whether they stood all round the tent is doubted by three sources, Ellicott denying the phrase requires it, Keil and Delitzsch reading a semicircle before the front, Calvin declining to count them eighteen a side. Wesley notices that they are still called seventy though two were missing, as the apostles are called the twelve when one is absent.

What their prophesying amounted to is disputed. Clarke grounds it in the verb, which he says means to pray and entreat, so that a prophet supplicates toward God and exhorts toward man, and reads their prophesying as the discharge of their new duties. Ellicott notes the word need not mean prediction and is elsewhere used of celebrating God's praise, and renders the closing clause not that they did not cease but that they did so no more. On that clause Wesley and Calvin flatly divide, Wesley holding the Spirit took up a settled abode because the gift's use was perpetual, Calvin that it was temporary and served as credentials, as prophecy did for Saul.

Why Eldad and Medad stayed in the camp nobody knows, and the sources guess differently. Henry reports the common view that they declined out of modesty, judging their principle their praise and their disobedience their fault, while Calvin doubts the summons ever found them and thinks God excused their ignorance. All agree the absence was providential, Henry because it proved the Spirit God's gift and not Moses', Calvin because the miracle then happened where the common people could see it. Keil and Delitzsch draw another inference from the phrase about those who were written, taking the summons to have been issued in writing and finding evidence of how thoroughly Israel had learned the art in Egypt.

Gill reports the rabbinic guess, from Jarchi, that the young man who ran with the news was Gershom, the son of Moses. Keil and Delitzsch explain Joshua's reaction from his position, a servant from his youth seeing authority conferred without his master's mediation as a slight, and compare his jealousy with the disciples' for Christ. Ellicott makes the same comparison and answers it alike, that as the man casting out devils acted in Christ's name, so these two prophesied by a Spirit whose giver was not Moses. Henry, supposing Joshua one of the seventy and so jealous for the order, draws four rules from the rebuke, against grieving at other men's gifts, against heat over their infirmities, against making the best men heads of a party, and against silencing those who do not follow with us.

Moses' reply admits two constructions, and Calvin chooses the simpler, that Moses is not saying the loss would be his own to grieve over but showing how differently he feels. He finds the gentleness of a man whom no thought of his own dignity kept from admitting the lowliest, though he notes Joshua's error sprang from a good source, a fear that any diminishing of Moses would dissipate God's grace. Wesley catches the precision of the wish, that Moses says prophets and not rulers, and draws the lesson that we should be glad God is glorified even at the cost of our own honour. Clarke answers with poetry rather than comment, printing Charles Wesley's hymns on the passage and remarking how notable such sentiments are from a man otherwise strict about ecclesiastical order.
31:
Gill and Ellicott both harmonise the account with the psalm, which names an east wind and a south wind, and settle on a south-east wind such as the Jewish writers describe. Keil and Delitzsch make it blow from the Arabian Gulf, bringing birds that fly north from the interior of Africa in spring in very great numbers. Clarke agrees the wind was no natural cause and cites Hasselquist, the pupil of Linnaeus, who saw great companies of quails in Egypt at just that season. Wesley adds that quails had been sent once before but neither in that quantity nor to that end, and that heathen writers report them thick on both sides of the Red Sea.

Whether the birds lay two cubits deep or flew two cubits high is the sharpest dispute in the chapter. Clarke rejects the common notion of a carpet of quails two feet thick, saying the Hebrew will not bear it, and follows the Vulgate in having them fly within reach of a man's club. Ellicott sets both readings out, objecting that heaped birds would need miraculous preserving since Israel might not eat what died of itself, yet granting the more obvious sense is a covering two cubits deep. Wesley proposes a middle course, that they fell round the camp for a day's journey on either side and lay in great heaps often two cubits high, and Henry remarks that locusts once a plague to fruitful Egypt would be a blessing in a barren wilderness.

Henry reads the gathering as a picture of appetite, that they flew on the spoil two days and a night without regarding the warning, and compares them unfavourably with David, who would not drink water won at hazard. Clarke explains the labour practically, that wearied flocks kept succeeding one another so speed was needed, and cites Maillet for the Egyptian way of curing such birds in hot sand, which he thinks is what spreading them abroad means. Wesley defends the ten homers on four grounds, that the gatherers acted for households, that they laid in a store rather than a meal, that the word may mean heaps and ten may mean many, and that a hundred thousand a day were once taken within five miles in Italy. Ellicott gives the measure, a homer of five or six bushels by rabbinic reckoning and about double by Josephus.

On the plague the sources divide over cause. Keil and Delitzsch expressly refuse the explanation that quails feed on matter injurious to man and their flesh brings on convulsions, insisting on an extraordinary judgment. Ellicott takes the opposite view, that such a surfeit would naturally produce much sickness and that here, as in the plagues of Egypt, the natural and supernatural are combined, while Clarke declines to determine what the writer left unsaid. Wesley asks why the same complaint was spared in Exodus and punished here, and answers that this came not of necessity but of wantonness, after manna, after long experience of God's care, and after the law was given.

Calvin fixes on the timing, that God did not wait until fullness turned to disgust but struck while the meat was in their mouths, since a belly may swell without the lust of eating being appeased. Henry gives it a colder edge, that God satisfied them before plaguing them so none could say he lacked power to supply them, and that this is what the prosperity of sinners means, since an ox is fed before the slaughter. Clarke turns from history to the reader, that these are Jude's murmurers and complainers, and that the greatest of prayers is thy will be done, since many petitions granted would be our ruin. The place-names close the chapter, Ellicott noting Taberah may have been part of Kibroth-hattaavah or another name for it, and Keil and Delitzsch that both sites are unknown.
